chapters.title: Fundamentals of Type I Hypersensitivity and Allergy Immunology
chapters.description: Overview of the immune mechanisms underlying immediate allergic reactions, including cellular players, antibody classes and signalling pathways that lead to rapid mediator release and systemic manifestations.
subtopics: Classification of hypersensitivity reactions (Gell and Coombs) with emphasis on immediate (Type I) reactions
Role of IgE, antigen presentation and sensitisation
Mast cell and basophil activation: FcεRI cross-linking and downstream signalling
Complement and other amplifying inflammatory pathways
Cytokines and chemokines in allergic inflammation
Clinical correlates of mediator effects (histamine, tryptase, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, platelet-activating factor)

chapters.title: Mast Cell Biology and Mediator Pharmacology
chapters.description: Anatomy, development and function of mast cells, their mediators and the systemic effects of mediator release relevant to anaphylaxis and mast cell disorders.
subtopics: Mast cell types, distribution and lifecycle
Preformed mediators (histamine, tryptase, heparin) and de novo mediators (leukotrienes, prostaglandins, cytokines)
Effects of mediators on vascular tone, permeability, bronchial smooth muscle and the nervous system
Regulation of mast cell activation and thresholds for degranulation
Laboratory detection of mediator release (tryptase, histamine, metabolites)
Pharmacologic targets to block mediator actions

chapters.title: Physiology and Pathophysiology of Cardiovascular and Respiratory Responses in Anaphylaxis
chapters.description: Cardiorespiratory mechanisms affected during anaphylaxis: how mediator release produces hypotension, bronchospasm, airway edema and hypoxaemia, and the physiologic rationale for therapeutic interventions.
subtopics: Normal cardiovascular and respiratory physiology relevant to shock and hypoxaemia
Vasodilation, increased vascular permeability and distributive shock mechanics
Bronchoconstriction and upper airway edema mechanisms
Effects on tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery
Compensatory responses and failure modes in severe anaphylaxis
Pathophysiologic distinctions between single-phase, biphasic, multiphasic and refractory courses

chapters.title: Clinical Presentation, Assessment and Early Recognition of Anaphylaxis
chapters.description: Typical and atypical clinical features of anaphylaxis across organ systems, structured clinical assessment, severity grading and initial triage principles.
subtopics: Diagnostic criteria for anaphylaxis (clinical features across airway, breathing, circulation, skin/mucosa, GI)
Common presenting symptoms and signs (urticaria, angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, GI symptoms, neurologic features)
Atypical presentations and pitfalls in recognition
Severity assessment scales and triage decisions
Initial monitoring requirements (vital signs, pulse oximetry, cardiac monitoring) and documentation
Initial differential diagnostic considerations

chapters.title: Emergency Pharmacology in Anaphylaxis: Epinephrine and Adjunctive Agents
chapters.description: Mechanisms of action, pharmacokinetics, dosing, routes of administration, adverse effects and practical considerations for epinephrine and commonly used adjunctive medications in anaphylaxis.
subtopics: Epinephrine pharmacodynamics: alpha-1, beta-1 and beta-2 effects and clinical implications
Recommended intramuscular dosing: 0.01 mg/kg (max 0.5 mg) and common auto-injector doses (0.15 mg, 0.3 mg, 0.5 mg); rationale for IM over other routes initially
Indications, techniques and dosing for intravenous epinephrine boluses and continuous infusions (when to escalate)
Antihistamines (H1 and H2): mechanisms, dosing and limits (symptomatic relief vs life-saving effect)
Bronchodilators (beta-2 agonists) for bronchospasm
Corticosteroids: mechanism, historical rationale for use in preventing biphasic reactions, and evidence base questioning routine use
Adjunctive measures: IV fluids, oxygen, vasopressors, glucagon in beta-blocked patients
Common adverse effects and monitoring during vasoactive therapy

chapters.title: Airway Management, Respiratory Support and Fluid Resuscitation in Anaphylactic Shock
chapters.description: Practical critical-care interventions for airway compromise and circulatory collapse in anaphylaxis, including indications and techniques for intubation, oxygen delivery, and volume resuscitation.
subtopics: Assessment for impending airway obstruction and indications for early intubation
Techniques for airway management in angioedema (awake intubation, surgical airway backup)
Oxygen delivery methods and escalation (nasal cannula, non-rebreather, non-invasive ventilation, mechanical ventilation)
Guidelines for initial fluid resuscitation volumes and rationale (crystalloids vs colloids)
Use of vasopressors and inotropes beyond epinephrine
Monitoring hemodynamic response and tissue perfusion in shock

chapters.title: Biphasic, Multiphasic and Refractory Anaphylaxis: Definitions, Epidemiology and Risk Factors
chapters.description: Definitions used in practice and research for biphasic, multiphasic and refractory anaphylaxis, reported incidence, candidate risk factors, and limitations of existing evidence.
subtopics: Operational definitions: biphasic vs multiphasic vs refractory anaphylaxis
Reported incidence ranges and methodological reasons for variability
Suggested predictors and risk factors (delay in epinephrine, severe initial reaction, multiple doses, patient factors)
Time course patterns and typical windows for recurrence (hours to days)
Evidence limitations and influence on clinical observation policies
Implications for monitoring strategies and resource allocation

chapters.title: Diagnostic Laboratory Testing in Suspected Anaphylaxis and Mast Cell Activation
chapters.description: Appropriate laboratory tests during and after anaphylaxis, optimal timing for sampling, interpretation of tryptase and other biomarkers, and practical constraints in the acute setting.
subtopics: Tryptase biology: sources, kinetics after mast cell activation and baseline considerations
Recommended sampling schedule for tryptase (acute sample ideally within 1–2 hours of symptom onset, peak within 1–4 hours, and baseline ≥24 hours after resolution)
Interpretation of elevated tryptase: relative vs absolute increases and thresholds suggestive of mast cell activation or systemic mastocytosis
Other laboratory tests: histamine/metabolites, complete blood count, lactate, arterial blood gas, electrolytes
Limitations: timing, stability, assay variability and differential diagnoses causing elevated tryptase
Reporting and documentation for later specialist review

chapters.title: Mast Cell Disorders: Systemic Mastocytosis and Mast Cell Activation Syndromes
chapters.description: Pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, diagnostic criteria, genetic markers, histopathology and management principles for systemic mastocytosis and related disorders that predispose to severe anaphylaxis.
subtopics: Classification of mast cell disorders (cutaneous mastocytosis, systemic mastocytosis, mast cell activation syndrome)
WHO diagnostic criteria for systemic mastocytosis: major and minor criteria overview
Role of KIT mutations (eg, D816V) and other molecular markers
Typical organ involvement (skin, bone marrow, liver, spleen, GI tract) and clinical manifestations
Bone marrow biopsy and histopathologic findings (mast cell aggregates, CD25/CD2 expression, morphology)
Implications of mast cell disorders for anaphylaxis risk, monitoring and long-term management

chapters.title: Allergy Diagnostics and Drug Hypersensitivity Workup
chapters.description: Principles and methodologies for diagnosing IgE-mediated and non-IgE-mediated drug allergies, including skin testing, in vitro assays and drug provocation testing, with attention to risks and contraindications.
subtopics: Types of drug hypersensitivity (immediate vs delayed) and mechanisms
Skin prick testing and intradermal testing: methodology, interpretation and safety considerations
Serologic testing (specific IgE) for drugs and other allergens: utility and limitations
Drug challenge/provocation testing: indications, contraindications and safety precautions
Approach to antibiotic allergy (beta-lactam testing algorithms, cross-reactivity concepts)
When to defer testing and referral pathways to allergy specialists

chapters.title: Diagnostic Imaging and Organ Assessment in Suspected Systemic Disease
chapters.description: Role of focused imaging and organ-specific tests to evaluate systemic conditions associated with mast cell disorders and to exclude alternative causes of symptoms.
subtopics: Ultrasound assessment (hepatomegaly, splenomegaly) and its role in systemic disease evaluation
Cross-sectional imaging (CT, MRI) indications for organomegaly or complications
Cardiac investigations in anaphylaxis (ECG changes, troponin considerations, myocardial dysfunction)
Pulmonary imaging for airway/aspiration complications
Use of bone marrow biopsy and interpretation alongside imaging findings
Limitations and timelines for imaging in the acute vs elective setting

chapters.title: Histopathology, Flow Cytometry and Molecular Diagnostics in Haematologic/Mast Cell Disorders
chapters.description: Laboratory methods used to identify clonal mast cell disease, including histopathologic assessment, immunophenotyping and molecular testing, and how these inform diagnosis and prognosis.
subtopics: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy: technique and key histologic findings
Immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry markers (CD117, CD25, CD2) on mast cells
Molecular testing for KIT mutations and other relevant genomic alterations
Correlation of laboratory and histologic findings with WHO diagnostic criteria
Reporting standards and interpretation in the context of incomplete sampling
Implications for treatment choices and specialist referral

chapters.title: Critical Care Management of Refractory and Severe Anaphylaxis
chapters.description: Advanced treatments and monitoring strategies used in intensive care for patients with refractory anaphylaxis, hemodynamic instability or recurrent episodes, including continuous vasopressor therapy and supportive measures.
subtopics: Definition and recognition of refractory anaphylaxis requiring ICU-level care
Indications for continuous intravenous epinephrine infusion: initiation, titration and monitoring
Second-line vasopressors and adjunctive drugs (norepinephrine, vasopressin, glucagon) in special populations
Hemodynamic monitoring (invasive and non-invasive) and goals of resuscitation
Management of multiple relapses: strategies, risks and benefits of preemptive infusion vs watchful waiting
Multidisciplinary care coordination (allergy, hematology, ICU) and escalation policies

chapters.title: Differential Diagnosis of Acute Hypotension, Flushing and Urticaria
chapters.description: Non-allergic and allergic conditions that mimic anaphylaxis, with clinical and investigational features to help distinguish them in the acute setting.
subtopics: Septic and distributive shock: distinguishing features (infectious source, inflammatory markers, fever)
Vasovagal syncope and orthostatic hypotension
Carcinoid syndrome and vasoactive tumor syndromes (clinical clues, biochemical testing)
Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma presentations with flushing and hemodynamic instability
Acute mast cell activation vs chronic urticaria and other dermatologic conditions
Drug-induced reactions unrelated to IgE (anaphylactoid/non-IgE mediated) and their recognition

chapters.title: Epidemiology, Risk Stratification and Clinical Guidelines for Observation After Anaphylaxis
chapters.description: Population-level data on anaphylaxis and guidance-based approaches to post-event observation, risk stratification and follow-up planning, including variability among international guidelines.
subtopics: Incidence and common triggers of anaphylaxis in different populations
Reported incidence and timing of biphasic reactions and factors affecting estimates
Risk-stratified observation recommendations from major organizations (eg, WAO, Resuscitation Councils, national guidelines) and rationale
Practical observation periods and criteria for admission vs discharge
Strategies to balance patient safety with healthcare resource utilization
Follow-up pathways: allergy referral, patient education and provision of emergency medications

chapters.title: Patient Education, Long-term Management and Legal/Practical Aspects of Anaphylaxis Care
chapters.description: Non-acute aspects of care: prescribing and training in epinephrine auto-injector use, lifestyle advice, written action plans, documentation and medicolegal considerations for follow-up of patients with anaphylaxis or suspected mast cell disorders.
subtopics: Indications for prescribing epinephrine auto-injectors and choosing appropriate dose/device
Patient education and demonstration of auto-injector use; written anaphylaxis action plans
Medication review and avoidance strategies for implicated triggers (drug labeling, alternatives)
Referral to allergy and haematology/mast cell disorder specialists and timelines
Documentation, communication with primary care and occupational/safety considerations
Ethical and medicolegal responsibilities in counselling about risks of re-exposure and risk mitigation
